title: The table of sinners
hook: in her last darkness, Thérèse pulls up a chair beside those who can't believe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse found her place: my vocation is love. Your line was love in the heart of the church. Which small thing did you do with love, and did anyone notice? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.
screen: `LOVE IN THE HEART OF THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: A sheet of paper, folded small, tucked inside a little book of the Gospels. Tradition says Thérèse of Lisieux copied the Creed onto it, the Church's own statement of faith, and kept it close in her last illness. Why would a nun whose whole life was built around prayer need to carry the Creed around like a note in a pocket? Because, in her last months, believing had stopped feeling like anything at all. She called it darkness. And she gave it a strange address, a place where she had been seated. Today, the table of sinners.
screen: `A CREED, FOLDED SMALL.` → `BELIEVING FEELS LIKE NOTHING.` → `A SEAT AT A STRANGE TABLE.`

segments.voice: First, the darkness. In the last part of her notebooks, written for her prioress, Thérèse says the thought of heaven, which had once been sweet to her, went dark. She writes of a thick fog. When she tried to rest her heart in that thought, the darkness seemed to mock her. She kept praying. She kept her duties. Second, the surprise. She admits that before this, she could hardly believe there were people with no faith at all. She had assumed they were speaking against what they really thought. Now she understood that some might honestly see nothing. The darkness taught her to take them seriously. Third, the table. Here is her image. She calls those who cannot believe her brothers. She says she is seated at their table, eating the bread of sorrow with them, and she will not ask to get up until the Lord says so. And from that chair she prays for everyone at the table together, asking mercy for us, not for them. It echoes the man at the back of the temple in Jesus's parable, who prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." Some readers say this one page changes how they hear the rest of her book. The Little Flower knew the dark from the inside. She did not lecture the people at that table. She sat down. And she held on to a cry from Mark's Gospel that belongs to anyone in that chair, a father with a sick son who says: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief."
screen: `THE THOUGHT OF HEAVEN GOES DARK.` · `SHE TAKES UNBELIEF SERIOUSLY.` · `SEATED AT THEIR TABLE, AS FAMILY.` · then, large: `I DO BELIEVE, LORD: HELP MY UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who can't believe. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person for whom faith is closed, or painful, or simply not there. A friend, a parent, a child, maybe a corner of yourself. Don't argue with them in your head. Don't plan a speech. Just pull up a chair beside them, the way Thérèse did, and sit. Let the quiet be shared. If you pray, you can say for both of you the father's words: help my unbelief. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind, with respect. The bell holds the time.
The table of sinners. Thérèse's image for her last darkness: seated beside those who can't believe, sharing their bread, and praying for everyone at the table. Today's word.
Your line: the table of sinners. Today, if someone speaks of doubt, don't rush to fix it. Listen like someone who shares their table. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics read Thérèse's account of her trial of faith in Story of a Soul, and some ask her prayers for people who struggle to believe, or pray for them in her spirit.

what it means: in her last months Thérèse felt only darkness, and chose to sit with unbelievers as family, praying for all of them.
what a scholar hears: the last notebook of Story of a Soul, where the trial of faith is told through the tax collector's prayer, mercy for us, not for them.
